news.title: The young Maga women whitewashing Trump's presidency
news.text:
The make-up of Donald Trump’s inner circle has come under scrutiny after US Senator Jon Ossoff remarked on the President’s close relationship with his executive assistant, Natalie Harp.

The White House fired back at his comments about Trump simply wanting to “travel with Natalie“, calling Harp, 35, “one of the most loyal and hardest-working aides on President Trump’s team”. 

The clash highlighted how Trump has surrounded himself with young, perfectly groomed Maga women in the White House, with the President regularly referring to their good looks and admiring their spirited defences of his policies.

Harp has reportedly taken on a role as the 80-year-old’s “comfort blanket” and “gatekeeper”, who leaves him adoring notes telling him “I want to bring you joy”. But he is also regularly flanked by the likes of “White House influencer” Margo Martin, 30, and deputy press secretary Anna Kelly, a 29-year-old former beauty queen.

The First Lady, Melania Trump, made a poised appearance in the days that followed Ossoff’s comments about Harp, indicating that she was unconcerned by the rumour mill. But as with Trump’s deeply loyal cabinet – both men and women – his youthful aides are raising genuine concern because of the part they play as enablers, whose sycophantic behaviour could help to legitimise the President’s most extreme actions.

Karoline Leavitt

Karoline Leavitt, 28, has been perhaps the most prominent of these women as White House press secretary and Trump’s most public defender. She recently announced she would step down at the end of August to focus on her family, but she will rejoin the pro-Trump super PAC Maga Inc as a top outside adviser.

Leavitt, who has served as press secretary since the beginning of Trump’s second term in January 2025, became the youngest person to ever hold the position at 27. She is known for her combative style and quick thinking – with some describing her as Trump’s “attack dog” – as well as for pushing false claims, including a notorious one about USAid using taxpayer money to fund $50m-worth of condoms in Gaza.

And her political ambitions may just be beginning. Announcing her departure on Truth Social, the President said that she would remain one of his “top advisers, and an influential voice within the Republican Party”. Before serving in the White House, Leavitt was the Republican nominee for the US House of Representatives in New Hampshire’s 1st congressional district in 2022, with Trump giving his enthusiastic endorsement.

Trump has said she is “one of the best” presidential press secretaries in history, and described her as one of his “most trusted aides”. She has repeatedly criticised “liberal media”, trolled journalists, and would often open press briefings with hyperbolic monologues praising her boss. “She’s become a star,” Trump said last year. “It’s that face, it’s that brain, it’s those lips – the way they move, they move like she’s a machine gun.”

Margo Martin

Margo Martin, communications adviser and special assistant to Trump, has been tipped as a possible replacement for Leavitt.

Leavitt said in an interview that the 30-year-old “has the trust of the President”, and “she’s able to really see the inner workings of his every day and share that with the American public”.

Martin, who has become the President’s leading content creator, has been called the “first White House influencer”. Like Harp, she is never far from Trump’s side, posting photo dumps and reels from Air Force One, international visits and high-level summits, including video from Trump’s Alaska summit with Vladimir Putin, which was criticised by Azza Cohen, Kamala Harris’s official White House videographer, for “whitewashing and sanitising”.

At a campaign rally, Trump called her “the most beautiful photographer in the world”. 

Martin grew up in Oklahoma and was the President’s press assistant during his first term. She also served as deputy director of communications for his Save America PAC. More than 300 high-profile right-wing organisations, influencers and politicians, including Elon Musk, the Republican National Committee and Fox News, have mentioned Martin since the inauguration in January 2025, sharing her posts thousands of times, according to analysis by The Washington Post.

Anna Kelly is also in the running to replace the outgoing Leavitt, who she has worked under as White House deputy press secretary. The 29-year-old is a former beauty queen with a master’s in political management, and was previously the national press secretary for the Republican National Committee.

Kelly was raised in Fairfax, Virginia, by parents who were “politically outspoken”. She began working as a campaign intern for a local Virginia Republican committee when she was in her mid-teens, before working as communication director for Republican Representative Derrick Van Orden of Wisconsin.

She is a Trump loyalist and has followed Leavitt in attacking journalists – branding The Hill’s White House correspondent Niall Stanage a “left-wing opinion writer hack” – and is quick to label “fake news”.

During a recent interview on The Clay Travis & Buck Sexton Show, Kelly described “winning every single day” at the White House and “having so much fun” working with the US President.

Kate Andersen Brower, the author of The Confidantes, a forthcoming book on women who have served as personal secretaries to US presidents, told the Financial Times that Trump “uses these younger women in his orbit as people who will really make him feel better”.

Natalie Harp

Harp has been dismissively nicknamed Trump’s “human printer” because of her habit of carrying a portable printer around with which to print out news articles and social media posts for her boss. But she has far more power than that, and is trusted with typing out his Truth Social posts, among other logistical responsibilities.

Harp had an unusual path to the White House. She grew up in a conservative Christian family in California, and after attending Point Loma Nazarene University in southern California, she received an MBA from Liberty University, a Christian university in Virginia.

She has long been infatuated with Trump – and credits him with saving her life. When Trump entered the White House in 2017, she was diagnosed with bone cancer. During his first term, he enacted a law to facilitate government approval of experimental drugs, which she then used to treat her cancer. 

She rose to prominence within the Maga movement by talking about her experience and was invited to speak at the 2020 Republican National Convention. “When I failed the chemotherapies that were on the market, no one wanted me in their clinical trials,” she said at the convention. “They didn’t give me the right to try experimental treatments. Mr President, you did, and without you, I’d have died waiting for them to be approved.”

Harp went on to host a show at the conservative One America News Network, or OAN – where she promoted false claims that Trump won the 2020 election – before joining his presidential campaign in 2022.

Her brother, Preston Harp, told CNN that her “dream came true” when she got the job at the White House and that his sister was Trump’s “biggest fan, so that’s probably why he likes her”.

“She thinks that he saved her life, so somebody living with that kind of gratitude must feel pretty good,” he added. “Trump is like everything that my mom taught us to respect. 

“So I think that’s where her infatuation for Trump comes from, honestly.

“My mom raised us with the idea that American exceptionalism was the correct way of looking at things. That the United States is the boss of the world. My sister, unfortunately, didn’t break out of that delusion.”

The President and Harp have a very close working relationship. Reporters Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan wrote in their book Regime Change that Trump told staff that she “was the only one who loved him as much as his wife and kids”.

She reportedly left him notes saying, “you are all that matters to me”, and, “I want to bring you joy”.

Ossoff made his comments after it emerged that Harp was one of the few aides who went with the President when he secretly switched planes after a Nato summit in Turkey last month, because of a possible Iranian threat.

“I’ve heard [Harp] referred to as his security blanket,” the rising Democratic star said on MS Now when asked about why he name-checked her. “And I think we could say that about any number of the senior aides in the White House. They’re not telling him what he needs to hear.”
news.author: Jessie Williams

news.title: Donald Trump Looks Like 'Open Can of Spam' Without Orange Bronx Bronzer, Anthony Scaramucci Claims
news.text: Donald Trump was spotted looking distinctly orange at a White House event as his former communications director delivered critical remarks on his morning beauty routine. The US President stepped into the Rose Garden on Monday sporting a deep, glowing hue to champion his administration's latest back-to-school initiatives. Anthony Scaramucci has now lifted the lid on the secret behind the legendary tan, claiming the president looks even worse without his daily cosmetics.According to the interview, criticism from Scaramucci's mother, a make-up artist, resulted in an extraordinary revelation. Speaking to The Times, the former aide shared that she hates the cosmetics. He explained, 'It's like an orange bronzer he buys from a supply shop in the Bronx. He looks like an open can of Spam without make-up.'The Secret Behind Donald Trump's Bronx BronzerScaramucci noted that the president puts it on in the morning and sometimes reapplies it at night. 'It's a tanner. He thinks it looks fantastic, by the way,' he told the publication. The canned meat, introduced to America in 1937, is recognisable for its characteristic light pink colour straight out of the can. The product develops a golden-brown or reddish-brown shade when fried, grilled or baked.Speculation surrounding the skin tone of the businessman has circulated for decades. The president has previously addressed his critics by attributing his complexion to energy-efficient lightbulbs.At a 2019 House Republican retreat dinner, he said: 'People said what's with the light bulb? I said here's the story, and I looked at it. The bulb that we're being forced to use, no.1, to me, most importantly, the light's no good. I always look orange.' That explanation has not prevented critics from bestowing upon him mocking nicknames, including 'Mango Mussolini' and 'Agent Orange'.Anthony Scaramucci Details Short White House TenureThe sharp commentary underscores how the relationship soured. Scaramucci had been a vocal critic before the businessman declared his candidacy in 2015. During the 2016 Republican Party primaries, he initially backed Scott Walker, then shifted support to Jeb Bush. After both candidates dropped out, he joined the Trump operation on finance and transition teams.He received an appointment as White House communications director in July 2017, serving for 11 days at the start of the first term. The stint ended after he conducted an off-the-record conversation with The New Yorker, where he harshly criticised White House colleagues Reince Priebus and Steve Bannon. He was swiftly dismissed by Chief of Staff John Kelly, with the blessing of the president.Former Aide Anthony Scaramucci Slams Donald TrumpScaramucci maintained his public allegiance until the summer of 2019, after which he reverted to being an outspoken critic. He threw his support behind Joe Biden in 2020 and Kamala Harris in 2024. The financier turned political commentator has since restored his standing on the podcast The Rest is Politics US. The news came after the president let slip his fury at outgoing press secretary Karoline Leavitt.Having worked in close proximity, the former aide is positioned to discuss what the president is genuinely like in private. During his interview with The Times, he asserted that nobody he has encountered genuinely likes the man. He stated: 'I have yet to find a person that really likes Trump. Including all of his family members. Nobody likes him.'He went on to reveal that his wife Deidre shares a similarly dim view, noting: 'My wife hates Trump almost as much as Melania. And if she was here, she would say more than Melania.

news.title: Jelly Roll sends message to MAGA fans threatening to boycott over Trump jokes
news.text:
Jelly Roll is not fazed by fans who were surprised by his mocking of Donald Trump during his guest-hosting stint on Jimmy Kimmel Live! this week.

On Monday, the rapper-turned-country music star made ruthless jabs at the president’s weight gain in his opening monologue.

The barbs surprised some who assumed the “Need A Favor” singer was a Republican due to his country roots.

On Tuesday night’s episode of Kimmel’s talk show, the rapper shared a headline from The Wrap, titled: “Jelly Roll Stuns ‘Jimmy Kimmel Live’ Audience With Multiple Jabs at Trump: ‘Didn’t See This Coming’.” 

“It’s because I’m hosting a damn late-night show. That’s where you talk about the news, and you make jokes,” he responded.

“I have to say, as a former felon, drug dealer who has lost 300 pounds, has tattoos all over his face and won three Grammys, this is the weirdest thing I’ve ever done to stun people.”

“Some folks online were upset that I didn’t treat the president with reverence and dignity. But I want to remind y’all that I go by the name Jelly Roll,” he said.

“I don’t even treat myself with reverence and dignity,” he joked. “One day I looked in the mirror and said, ‘You, my friend, are a pastry.’ Frankly, I think most people were just surprised that I had any opinions at all. They see a guy that looks like me and assume the only opinion I have is whether I prefer my meth crystal or classic.”

Jelly Roll on Monday spoke about his friendship with Kimmel — who is one of the president’s staunchest critics — and has previously said he has “no political alliance.”

The rapper went on to poke more fun at the president, saying Tuesday, “Now, let’s be honest for a second. Any U.S. president should be able to handle a few jokes, right? They should also be able to handle gas prices, healthcare, and the occasional international conflict, but that can’t be true.

“Look, y’all, I get it that some people are mad at me for goofing on Trump, but if you wanted me to make jokes about Kamala Harris, you should have voted for her,” he quipped.

The star added, “Who would have guessed I’d get in more trouble with the president than Rosie O’Donnell?”

Trump’s longtime nemesis O’Donnell hosted Kimmel last week, although she largely steered clear of the president in her monologues.

“So, for those who threatened to stop listening to my music based on my comments last night,” Jelly Roll continued, “I just want to say with conviction: go right ahead, ‘cause I’m going to keep speaking my truth, or my name isn’t Post Malone.”
news.summary: Tennessee rapper shocked some fans who assumed he was a supporter of the Republican president
news.author: Tom Murray

news.title: Arizona recorder's election-denying allies boost legislative campaign
news.text:
Maricopa County Recorder Justin Heap’s allies are financially supporting a lawyer from Stephen Miller’s firm running for the Arizona Legislature, all while the attorney landed Heap a major victory in his push to gain more power over elections in the battleground state's most populous county. 

Heap’s network is boosting Republican James Rogers’ bid for a state House seat in the East Valley. Rogers is senior counsel at America First Legal, the law firm co-founded by President Donald Trump’s adviser Miller.

He also represented Heap in his high-profile election battle with the Maricopa County Board of Supervisors.

The Rogers' campaign finance report shows how a network of Republicans who challenged the 2020 election results and gained power in Arizona and are seeking more influence at the ballot box this November. 

“He's an election-denier, and his whole circle is election-deniers,” said Tyler Montague, a Republican anti-Trump activist from Mesa, where Heap and Rogers both live. 

Rogers was instrumental in Heap’s election dispute victory in Maricopa County, and records show that people affiliated with the recorder donated to the Rogers' campaign shortly after each of Rogers’ courtroom triumphs. 

Plus, Heap allies bitterly attacked Rogers' Republican opponent during the primary, dredging up unflattering details from her past and mocking her with AI-created memes. 

The result was a 13-percentage-point win for Rogers in the July 21 primary election. He’s likely to coast to victory in the safely red legislative district this fall and, with the backing of Turning Point Action, succeed Heap’s father in the Legislature. 

Heap's allies gave Rogers cash on key days

As Heap’s pro bono lawyer, Rogers is in the unique position of running for office in an election overseen by his client, while helping him fight to change the rules of the election. 

The county recorder and county supervisors share election administration duties in Maricopa County. Heap argued that the board usurped his power when it negotiated a shared-services agreement that pared back his responsibilities just before he took office. 

Rogers pulled papers to run for the state House on June 9, 2025. Three days later, Rogers filed Heap’s lawsuit against the board. 

The bitter legal feud lasted for more than a year and went through three courtrooms: Maricopa County Superior Court, the Arizona Court of Appeals and finally the Arizona Supreme Court. 

Rogers’ involvement in the case itself was controversial: Maricopa County Attorney Rachel Mitchell last year told him to stand down in a letter.

But Heap stuck with Rogers in the courtroom. He also praised him on the campaign trail.

“I have been nothing but humbled and amazed at his prowess and his dedication,” Heap told an “Election Integrity Rally” crowd days before the primary, taking a victory lap after Rogers helped him beat the supervisors in court. 

Heap made the speech in front of a sign that depicted Rogers as Fred Rogers from the children’s show “Mister Rogers' Neighborhood,” according to a video. Heap's office did not respond to a request for comment.

Election-deniers contributed to Rogers' campaign coffers

As the case progressed and Rogers notched courtroom victories, Heap’s staff and allies donated to his state representative campaign along the way, records show.

Two days after Judge Scott Blaney ruled in Heap’s favor on April 17, Rogers received $500 in campaign contributions from Merissa Caldwell, records show. She is married to Jeff Caldwell, Heap’s director of special projects. 

Merissa Caldwell is a far-right activist in her own right. She shares misinformation about elections and supports the Arizona Republicans who were charged with multiple felony counts after falsely certifying that Trump won the presidential election here in 2020.

She also serves as the head of Election Integrity Network’s Arizona chapter. The national group is overseen by Cleta Mitchell, an important player in Trump’s plot to overturn the 2020 election. 

Cleta Mitchell also donated to Rogers’ campaign. She gave him $500 on April 22, a few weeks after Rogers proposed that she serve as mediator in the dispute between Heap and the board on April 6. 

The board did not take Rogers up on the offer.

The next month, after a judge ruled again in favor of Heap on May 13, Rogers got $250 from Heap’s chief of staff. Sam Stone contributed on May 14, according to a campaign finance report. 

Merissa Caldwell gave Rogers another contribution on June 8, saying she and her husband, a top Heap staffer, would go without some extra cash to help him. 

“It's worth it to give up a few date nights with my husband to get James elected!” Merissa Caldwell wrote on X.

Two days earlier, the county had announced outside counsel would investigate why two members of Heap’s staff took voting equipment out of a county facility. Rogers was involved in that issue as part of the Board of Supervisors dispute, but he is not involved anymore, America First Legal spokesperson Dani Repass said in an email. 

Rogers’ most significant legal victory came the next month, when the Arizona Supreme Court sided on July 7 with his legal arguments and expanded Heap’s power over elections. 

Merissa Caldwell gave Rogers $1,000 that day, records show.

Two days later, on July 9, Rogers received $200 from Republican nominee for Secretary of State Alex Kolodin.

Kolodin also had given Heap legal advice in the Maricopa County dispute, according to the recorder’s office. 

“AFL was not aware of these donations until you raised them, and they had no bearing whatsoever on AFL’s legal work for Recorder Heap,” said Repass, the America First Legal spokesperson. 

Repass put some daylight between Rogers' campaign and his legal work. America First Legal is a 501c3 nonprofit that does not endorse candidates or engage in electoral politics, she said.

“AFL’s pro bono representation of Recorder Heap was based solely on the legal merits of his position, and nothing else. Mr. Rogers’ campaign is a personal endeavor entirely separate from his work at AFL, and AFL has no involvement in or control over his campaign’s fundraising,” Repass said.

The contributions did not raise major red flags for Brendan Galvin, the director of insights at the campaign finance watchdog group OpenSecrets. Heap’s allies did not appear to be coerced into giving the donations, he noted. 

“When you're within that community and one of your own is running for office and you have the ability to support them financially,” Galvin said. “It's not surprising to see that.” 

Even beyond Heap’s allies, the legal wins in Maricopa County were some of Rogers’ most lucrative fundraising days of the campaign, records show. 

“Just because it's technically OK doesn't make it ethically OK,” said Jennifer Guzman, the programs director for Common Cause Arizona, a left-leaning group. “This is really just a push to have more control over who gets a say in these elections.” 

Rogers declined to answer questions about donations from Heap's allies. He has taken on a number of cases in Arizona as a lawyer for America First Legal, where he has worked since 2023.

Rogers played up his election experience in a written statement.

"I am running for the Arizona House because I have the skills, experience, and backbone to help make Arizona permanently red," Rogers said in an email. "As an election integrity lawyer who has litigated these issues and has already drafted bills for the Legislature, I will be the only Representative with the specialized knowledge of election law to craft the reforms we need."

Heap allies slammed Rogers' Republican opponent 

The county recorder’s father, Republican state Rep. Ralph Heap, opened the door to a nasty political fight when he gave up his seat to seek a spot on the Arizona Corporation Commission this election cycle. 

Rogers won the primary with a boost from Turning Point Action, the political arm of the Phoenix-based conservative network. Ralph Heap is endorsed by Turning Point and embroiled in his own political drama after being accused of campaign finance violations.

Although she founded a Turning Point coalition, Rogers’ Republican opponent Ciara Anderson became the subject of attacks from the group’s leader and Heap allies in the run-up to Primary Day. 

The attacks followed an article by the State 48 News accusing Anderson of failing to "clearly disclose to voters" her bad conduct discharge from the Air Force, although Anderson’s campaign literature mentioned it. Christy Kelly, the writer behind the news site, told The Republic she had never been part of Rogers' campaign and her article was published independently of any political group or message.

Anderson did not respond to a request for comment. 

People shared AI-generated memes depicting Anderson as “woke” with blue hair and a Pinocchio-style growing nose.

Tyler Bowyer, Turning Point Action chief operating officer, used his platform to attack Anderson online, saying she “couldn’t be more disingenuous or ungrateful.” Reached for this story, Bowyer said he was unavailable for comment until January.

Bowyer is also tied to the election denier movement. He was indicted for his alleged role in Arizona’s 2020 fake electors scheme.

Bowyer pointed out online that Anderson had support from moderate Republicans. He said he was disappointed that Anderson did not do more to oust a Republican city council member in Mesa who supported Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential race. 

But perhaps no one was more passionately against Anderson than Merissa Caldwell, who bashed Anderson as a “complete lying charlatan” even after she lost. 

The Republic's Ray Stern contributed to this report.

Stephanie Murray covers national politics and the Trump administration for The Arizona Republic and azcentral.com. She co-hosts “The Gaggle,” The Republic’s weekly politics podcast. Reach her at stephanie.murray@usatodayco.com, on X and TikTok @stephanie_murr and on Instagram @stephaniemurray.news.
news.author: The Arizona Republic

news.title: Black Celebrities React to Dolly Parton’s Death
news.text:
As the world is still reeling over the news of legendary country music star Dolly Parton’s death, Black celebs and influential figures are speaking out and sending their love to the “9 to 5” singer.

Beyoncé, who recently collaborated with Parton for her 2024 album, “Cowboy Carter,” shared a touching tribute to the Queen of Country.

“Dolly, you were the barometer. The North Star. Bold and brilliant. Talented and tenacious. You taught so many lessons on how to be uniquely oneself. I am grateful for your art, your heart, your generosity, your humor, your entrepreneurship,” Bey wrote in her post.

She continued: “I’m honored that I had the privilege to work with you. I will treasure that forever. Thank you for your profound impact on the world. You are an angel who has made this world a happier place because of your joyful art. You are truly one of one. Rest peacefully.”

Related: 11 Reasons Why Black Folks Will Always Love Dolly Parton

Chaka Khan also paid her respects to Parton, writing on Instagram and Facebook, “A once-in-a-lifetime artist, songwriter, storyteller & generous spirit, Dolly gave the world music filled with heart, humor & grace. Her music will keep playing. Her light will keep shining.”

Fellow country music star Shaboozey reflected on Parton’s contributions and expressed sorrow that their paths never crossed.

“Rest in peace Dolly Parton, I wish I had the honor of meeting you. You were everyone’s favorite artist. Thank you for giving us some of the greatest music we’ll ever know,” he said in a post to X/Twitter.

Emmy-nominated actor Colman Domingo honored the “I Will Always Love You” singer, writing in a social media post: “Dolly taught us that you can be anything and do anything and to do it with kindness. What a light. We are all grateful that we lived in a time of Dolly Parton. We will always love her.”

Even politicians, including former President Barack Obama, reflected on Parton’s legacy.

“It’s hard to imagine many people having a bigger impact than Dolly Parton. Born in a one-room cabin, she earned 11 Grammys and an Emmy, built a business empire, helped millions of kids learn to read, and — as if that wasn’t enough — helped accelerate the research that led to the Moderna COVID vaccine. What a life. Michelle and I are thinking of Dolly’s family and her many, many fans,” he wrote in a post on X/Twitter.

Bernice A. King also spoke out on the “Jolene” singer, expressing her sadness over her death and remarking on her commitment to literacy and human rights issues.

“Her extraordinary voice entertained and brought joy to generations, and she used her influence beyond music to affirm human dignity, inclusion, and the importance of treating people with love and respect. Through her commitment to literacy, she also opened doors of possibility for children around the world,” she said in part.

Other notable Black celebrities, including former Vice President Kamala Harris, Jennifer Hudson, rapper Juicy J, Donna Brazile and Dionne Warwick, paid tribute to Parton and shared messages of support with her family.
news.summary:
From fellow country music stars like Shaboozey to actors like Colman Domingo, Black celebs are paying their respects to the late Dolly Parton.

news.title: GOP’s ‘Decoy Dan’ Sullivan advances with Sen. Dan Sullivan, possibly helping Dem foes
news.text:
WASHINGTON — An Alaskan Republican who shares the same name as the state’s incumbent, Sen. Dan Sullivan, advanced past the open primary for the seat Wednesday — worsening a muddled GOP situation that could boost Dems.

Retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan made the cut in Alaska’s open contest that is sending the top four candidates from either party on to the general election, according to multiple projections over a week after the Aug. 18 primary.

Sullivan — dubbed “Decoy Dan’’ for registering as a GOPer days before the primary — is joining GOP Sen. Dan S. Sullivan and Dem ex-Rep. Peltola in the final stretch. 

It was not immediately clear who the fourth candidate on the ballot will be.

Alaska’s general election in November will be ranked-choice voting. 

Peltola has been leading in polls of the critical Alaska Senate contest, despite the state typically leaning red.

Dan J. Sullivan has denied accusations that he is a Democratic plant seeking to siphon votes from Sen. Sullivan by having the same name, thus boosting Peltola.

He insists that he’s a moderate Republican, despite telling the New York Times that he voted for the Democratic nominee in the last three presidential cycles, attended at least one “No Kings” protest, and backed Peltola in both her congressional campaigns.

The Last Frontier state last picked a Democrat for Senate in 2008, but Peltola managed to flip Alaska’s at-large US House seat in 2022, proving that she is a force to be reckoned with in statewide races.

Democrats see Alaska as one of their top four pick-up opportunities for the Senate this cycle alongside Maine, Ohio and North Carolina.

Complicating things for the Republicans has been Dan J. Sullivan’s inclusion on the ballot.

While a lower court judge initially kicked him off the ballot, citing evidence that he wasn’t mounting “an actual good-faith candidacy,” the Alaska Supreme Court let him back on.

The lower court judge had knocked “Decoy Dan” for registering as a Republican days before filing his candidacy.

Peltola’s campaign has meanwhile been hit by recent turbulence.

Earlier this month, Peltola ignited controversy when her campaign said it didn’t approve of former Vice President Kamala Harris’ fundraising message in support of her Senate bid.

Harris had urged her supporters to back Peltola, who is trying to win in a state that the former veep lost by about 14 percentage points.

Afterward, Peltola lost several senior campaign officials in what her team described as a shake-up to prepare for the general election.

She has been trying to run as a centrist-type Democrat in her effort to appeal to Alaska’s famously maverick voters.

Peltola has a 2-percentage-point edge over Sen. Sullivan in the latest RealClearPolitics aggregate of polls in a hypothetical two-way matchup.
news.summary: Retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan made the cut in Alaska’s open contest that is sending the top four candidates from either party on to the general election, according to multiple projections.
news.author: Ryan King

news.title: Even Iowa? Trump's troubles tighten races for Senate, governor
news.text:
Even in Iowa, Republican candidates for the Senate and governorship are now locked in tight races, a new Suffolk University poll finds − thanks in part to dissatisfaction with Donald Trump in a state he carried in three presidential elections.

The margin-of-error results in the Hawkeye State are stoking Democratic hopes of scoring midterm victories in unexpected places.

In the governor's race, Democratic state Auditor Rob Sand is leading Republican businessman Zach Lahn by 4 percentage points, 48%-44%.

In the Senate race, Republican congresswoman Ashley Hinson is leading Democratic state representative Josh Turek by 4 points, 45%-41%.

“Keep in mind this is a state that Donald Trump won by more than 13 points in 2024,” said David Paleologos, director of the Suffolk University Political Research Center in Boston. No Democrat has been elected governor of Iowa in 20 years, and none has been elected to the Senate in 18.

The poll of 500 likely voters, taken Aug. 20-23 by landline and cell phone, has an error margin of plus or minus 4.4 points.

Asked their "primary motivation" for voting in the midterm election, 30% said it was to "express dissatisfaction with the current national political climate." That's more than the number who cited supporting a specific candidate's vision (11%) and weighing in on local ballot issues (16%), combined.

Four in 10 said they were voting to "fulfill my civic duty."

In the governor's race, Sand has edged ahead thanks to near-solid support among Democrats, disproportionate support among independents (53%-34%) and even 9% support from Republicans. In contrast, Lahn received no Democratic support.

In the Senate race, Turek is supported by nearly all Democrats and leads narrowly among independents, 39%-35%, plus 5% of Republicans. Hinson was backed by a single Democratic respondent.

When the handful of Trump voters in 2024 who aren't supporting Hinson were asked why, the most common response was that Republicans had "gotten off track" and "didn't deliver."

Among the most enthusiastic voters, those very likely to vote, Turek and Hinson are tied, 45%-45%.

The race is being closely watched as an unexpected prospect to help Democrats regain control of the Senate. That would require holding all the Democratic-held seats on the ballot in November and flipping four Republican-held seats. Iowa hasn't been in the top tier of Democratic targets, but a competitive race here could help offset a loss elsewhere.

Sen. Joni Ernst isn't running for reelection. Nor is Gov. Kim Reynolds.

Iowa is still, to be clear, a ruby-red state. Registered Republicans outnumber Democrats by 200,000, and Republicans now hold all six seats in Congress, both chambers of the state legislature and every statewide elected office save one.

But the state's agricultural economy has been hit hard by trade wars and the rising costs of gas and fertilizer, and the national issues over the affordability of groceries, housing and health care resonate here, as well.

While Trump swamped Democrat presidential nominee Kamala Harris in Iowa in 2024, his favorable-unfavorable rating is now underwater by a tick, at 48%-49%.

Among Republicans, 10% now give him an unfavorable rating, and independents by 51%-42% have an unfavorable view.

To compare, former president Barack Obama, who carried Iowa in both his presidential campaigns, has a rating that is narrowly positive, 49%-45%.

The survey also showed the transformation in the way voters prefer to gather information about political campaigns. At the top were candidate debates and town halls, followed in close order by social-media platforms, then by local news broadcasts and newspapers.
news.author: Usa Today

news.title: ‘Kimmel’ Guest Host Jelly Roll Doubles Down On Trump Mockery After MAGA Backlash
news.text:
“Jimmy Kimmel Live” guest host Jelly Roll doubled down on mocking President Donald Trump during Tuesday night’s show, after waves of MAGA backlash. 

The rapper and singer kicked off his monologue by addressing the apparent shock many viewers expressed after Monday’s show, where Jelly Roll scorned the president for his fatphobic insults.

“You know what? I did a couple of jokes like that last night in case y’all didn’t hear about it, and it’s because I’m hosting a damn late-night show,” Jelly Roll said on Tuesday. “That’s where you talk about the news and you make jokes. But I guess apparently because I did it, it really messed with people’s heads.” 

Jelly Roll said he thought it was the “weirdest thing he’s ever done to stun people.” 

“Who would have guessed I’d get in more trouble with the president than Rosie O’Donnell?” Jelly Roll said. 

He added that many people online, mostly conservatives, were mad that he didn’t treat the president with respect. 

“Let’s be honest for a second. Any U.S. president should be able to handle a few jokes, right?” Jelly Roll said. “They should also be able to handle gas prices, healthcare, and the occasional international conflict.” 

The rapper also said if people wanted him to make fun of former Vice President Kamala Harris, they “should’ve voted for her.” 

Jelly Roll said he didn’t care if people stopped listening to his music because he made fun of Trump and that he will keep “speaking his truth.” 

Jelly Roll has often been perceived as conservative or a MAGA supporter due to his status as a country artist, but has said in the past he holds no political affiliation. 

“It is important to establish earlier that I am a musician and that I have no political alliance,” he said before Congress while giving testimony about the fentanyl crisis in 2024. “I am neither Democrat nor Republican. In fact, because of my past, my right to vote has been restricted. Thus far, I have never paid attention to a political race in my life. Ironically, I think that makes me the perfect person to speak about this.”

However, the rapper did meet then-President-elect Trump during a UFC event in December 2024. Jelly Roll defended meeting Trump at the time by saying he did it out of respect for the presidency. 

“I don’t care who you were, if you were in that building, the hair on your skin stood up,” he said. “And you looked, and all you’re watching is the president-elect, who got elected like, eight days ago, walking in, with his entire Cabinet with him — almost. You know what I mean? And his kids and his grandchildren. And it was powerful, dude. Like I don’t care what side of the aisle you’re on.”

Nonetheless, conservative figures on social media were none-too-pleased by Jelly Roll’s perceived betrayal of Trump. 

See reactions to Jelly Roll’s monologue on Monday as well as his full Tuesday monologue below
news.author: Anthony Orrico

Jelly Roll said he didn’t care if people stopped listening to his music because he made fun of Trump and that he will keep “speaking his truth.” 

Jelly Roll has often been perceived as conservative or a MAGA supporter due to his status as a country artist, but has said in the past he holds no political affiliation. 

“It is important to establish earlier that I am a musician and that I have no political alliance,” he said before Congress while giving testimony about the fentanyl crisis in 2024. “I am neither Democrat nor Republican. In fact, because of my past, my right to vote has been restricted. Thus far, I have never paid attention to a political race in my life. Ironically, I think that makes me the perfect person to speak about this.”

However, the rapper did meet then-President-elect Trump during a UFC event in December 2024. Jelly Roll defended meeting Trump at the time by saying he did it out of respect for the presidency. 

“I don’t care who you were, if you were in that building, the hair on your skin stood up,” he said. “And you looked, and all you’re watching is the president-elect, who got elected like, eight days ago, walking in, with his entire Cabinet with him — almost. You know what I mean? And his kids and his grandchildren. And it was powerful, dude. Like I don’t care what side of the aisle you’re on.”

Nonetheless, conservative figures on social media were none-too-pleased by Jelly Roll’s perceived betrayal of Trump.

news.title: Democratic Voters Reject Resistance Stars
news.text:
There has been a lot of commentary on the differences between Resistance 1.0, the effort by anti-Trump activists to bring down President Donald Trump in his first term, and Resistance 2.0, the effort by anti-Trump activists to bring down Trump in his second term. There are some tactical contrasts, but the simple fact is, they're still at it.

This year's election season has featured two much-lauded figures of Resistance 1.0 as they tried to use their anti-Trump agitation as a springboard to public office. Alex Vindman, the former National Security Council staffer who in 2019 set off the first Trump impeachment, ran for U.S. Senate in Florida, and George Conway, the lawyer who talked E. Jean Carroll into suing Trump, ran for the House in New York.

Both suffered crushing defeats in Democratic primaries.

Conway ran in New York's 12th Congressional District, in Manhattan, the seat vacated by the retirement of Democratic Rep. Jerry Nadler. There were a lot of candidates. Conway finished fifth, with 6.1% of the vote. A wealthy lawyer, Conway loaned his campaign $2 million for the run. In all, he spent $5.7 million.

The money allowed Conway to mount a vanity campaign, to publicly fantasize about getting Trump, and to pound his chest about the massive damage judgment against Trump in the Carroll trial. "Hi, Donald! It's me, George Conway," began one ad. "I cost you $88 million f*king dollars, and I've only just gotten started." For his next act, Conway promised to put Trump in jail.

Conway obviously thought the theme might work in New York's 12th, in which Kamala Harris beat Trump 81% to 17% in the 2024 presidential election. But of course all Democrats in the race promised to oppose Trump. The Democratic voters' job was to choose the best. Conway was not their first, second, third or fourth choice. Instead, the primary winner was a member of the New York state assembly named Micah C. Lasher, who pledged to stand up to Trump.

The other Resistance star to face-plant was Vindman, who in 2019, as an active-duty Army lieutenant colonel on the staff of the National Security Council, set in motion the first impeachment of Trump. Vindman, who was privy to some of the president's calls with world leaders, felt that Trump had committed some sort of unspecified violation in a conversation with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Vindman relayed secret information to a friend in the CIA, who came up with a "whistleblower" complaint against the president.

The impeachment failed, of course. Under pressure from the Trump administration, Vindman retired from the military and began trading on his notoriety. He wrote a memoir called "Here, Right Matters," with the title based on his congressional testimony. He started a company called Here Right Matters LLC. It did well; in a financial disclosure form this year, Vindman listed around $1.5 million in income from that and other ventures. The Alexander Vindman business did pretty well.

The next step would be politics. Vindman moved to Florida and ran for the Senate as a Democrat. When he jumped into the race in January, his announcement video began with news clips from his role in the Trump impeachment. A moment later, Vindman said, as pictures of his congressional testimony played: "The last time you saw me was here, swearing an oath to tell the truth about a president who broke his. See, my family came to America as refugees to escape tyranny. And I sure as hell was not going to bow down to some wannabe tyrant. This president unleashed a reign of terror and retribution, not just against me and my family, but against all of us."

No subtlety there; the Hero of the Resistance had arrived to take on Trump! Vindman raised $16 million for his campaign, while his Democratic socialist opponent, Angie Nixon, raised a little less than $1 million. Vindman immediately became a heavy favorite to win the Democratic nomination. He remained the favorite until Election Day, when Nixon shocked the political world by trouncing Vindman, 56% to 44%.

Once again, the Resistance 1.0 magic did not work. As it had been in Manhattan, only on a far larger scale, Florida Democratic voters just didn't care that a candidate had led one of the many unsuccessful efforts to drive Trump out of office from 2017 to 2021. That doesn't mean they like or support Trump; they absolutely don't. But it does mean that all the excitement that Conway and Vindman and their allies stirred up in the wayback time of Trump 1.0 truly came to nothing.

This content originally appeared on the Washington Examiner at washingtonexaminer.com/daily-memo/4695532/democratic-voters-reject-resistance-stars/.
news.author: Byron York

news.title: Why Gush Over Abdul El-Sayed Taking on 'Fox's Outrage Machine'?
news.text:
On Aug. 24, controversial Democrat Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed boldly accepted an invitation to the Fox News show "Jesse Watters Primetime." It oozed confidence, but whether it was smart or strategic to play the Artful Dodger is a very different question.

In his newsletter, CNN media analyst Brian Stelter gushed over El-Sayed generating "lots of buzz and clippable content" and how he "showed a keen understanding of Fox's outrage machine." This is always amusing, as if Stelter doesn't think CNN can be characterized as operating an "outrage machine" against Trump.

Then Stelter mischaracterized the central mishap of the interview. El-Sayed was credited for "refusing to take the bait when Watters asked whether it's okay 'for a parent to slash his kid's ding-a-ling off' or whether trans athletes should compete in women's sports. Each time, he redirected toward gas and grocery prices, the war in Iran, and health care."

That's not what happened. When Watters pressed him on genital amputations for children, he insisted this decision is between a doctor and a patient, and the government should not get involved — which is a bizarre position when you're pushing for a "Medicare for All" scheme where the government controls the health care system.

When Watters kept pressing, El-Sayed asked the host, "Do you really wanna have this conversation? Are you circumcised?" What kind of oafish inquiry is that? Then he pressed: "So you should want to move on." That's not answering the question. It's an attempt to shut down the line of inquiry by getting personal.

Watters felt compelled to point out to the guy who went to an Ivy League medical school that "circumcision is different than castration." El-Sayed just repeated, "It's a problem that you think that you get to decide what happens between a parent, a doctor and a patient." That's a questionable position, since El-Sayed fervently supported COVID lockdowns and vaccine mandates five years ago.

The host shifted into the scandal of boys playing in girls' sports, and that's when the Democrat started leaning into the high prices and the war, "the issues people actually care about in Michigan." Watters pointed out that the interview started with gas prices and the so-called Green New Deal.

Stelter touted similar analysis from a fellow liberal at The New York Times. Bayliss Wagner wrote El-Sayed's strategy was "to cast 'culture-war' issues as a distraction from the everyday problems Americans face, like rising costs and worries about health care."

The Left loves to play this dishonest game: "Culture wars" only start when conservatives resist the leftist crusade, and it's only a "distraction" when the Left doesn't win without a fight. They know the transgender issue was a reason Kamala Harris lost, so they want to dodge the issue.

Stelter concluded by telling readers to "beware the algorithmic distortion," with conservatives "celebrating Watters for dunking on El-Sayed and exposing Democratic 'extremism.'" They always pretend no Democrat position is extreme. Stelter added his CNN colleague Andrew Kirell "saw post after post from liberals applauding El-Sayed for showing how to handle Fox — by engaging and knowing all their tricks."

Stelter and his media colleagues are only grading El-Sayed on his tactical dodging skills around Fox "tricks." They're not examining how voters may want to know where the Democrat stands on amputations for kids, or boys in girls' sports. Candidates for office should have identifiable positions, not just dismiss "distractions."

This is the same Stelter who hailed Sen. Jon Ossoff's "art of the viral clip" for recklessly smearing White House aide Natalie Harp as Trump's new girlfriend. Why must they only judge tactics and not judge on the facts?

news.title: Wisconsin experts reject Census report claiming 500 noncitizen voters
news.text:
A newly released U.S. Census Bureau report claims 500 noncitizens voted in Wisconsin's 2020 general election, but election experts say there are serious issues with the report's data and methodology.

A Census Bureau report that calls itself a "beginning analysis" was released Aug. 18 and claims to have found 24,000 noncitizens nationwide who voted in the 2020 general election by comparing federal and third-party voter data.

Philip Rocco, a professor and chair of Marquette University's political science department, described the Census report as "meaningless."

"There are questions about data stewardship and data linkage from the very start, before we even get into more issues like authorship and citation," Rocco said. "This is not a Census Bureau product."

More: Wisconsin has dealt with election day problems dating back to 2011

State and federal law prohibit noncitizens in Wisconsin from voting in state or federal elections, according to the Wisconsin Elections Commission.

Emilee Miklas, a WEC spokesperson, declined to comment on the Census report, but told the Journal Sentinel there is "no evidence to indicate that a significant number of noncitizens have voted in previous elections or will do so in upcoming elections."

"Wisconsin has many systems in place to deter and detect illegal voting," Miklas said. "After every election, local election officials and the WEC conduct audits designed to identify possible cases of voter fraud, which are referred to district attorneys for further investigation and possible prosecution."

The state's voter database is designed to find any possible instances of double voting, Miklas added.

The state Division of Motor Vehicles, the Department of Corrections and the Electronic Registration Information Center all check the accuracy of voter registration through regular audits. Noncitizens are disqualified from voting in state and federal elections even if they have a valid driver's license.

There have been only a handful of voter fraud cases prosecuted in Wisconsin since 2020, and most were for double voting, not noncitizen voting.

Noncitizens attempting to vote in Wisconsin is extremely rare. The WEC has been made aware of only four alleged cases of election fraud tied to citizenship since 2015, and none took place during the 2020 election, the Journal Sentinel previously reported.

Census report claim would not change Wisconsin election outcomes

A difference of 500 votes would not have changed the outcome of any federal race in Wisconsin in 2020.

Joe Biden and Kamala Harris defeated Donald Trump and Mike Pence in Wisconsin by 20,608 votes. Democrat Ron Kind defeated Republican challenger Derrick Van Orden by 10,328 votes, the state's closest federal race that year.

On Aug. 18, President Donald Trump posted "I WON THE ELECTION!" on his Truth Social account and cited the new Census report. Trump also claimed the next Census report will show more evidence of voter fraud.

The Census Bureau said in the report that it already examined 128 million voter records and claims to have found 24,000 noncitizen voters nationwide in 2020. The report also claims 32 million voter records have yet to be analyzed.

2020 Elections: FBI interviews at least 2 Milwaukee police officers in 2020 probe

Data quality makes the new Census report 'worthless,' expert says

Rocco, the Marquette political science professor, said the report's data is "worthless" because of the way it's linked in an effort to show evidence of noncitizen voting.

Typically, researchers expect Census data to have a 1%-6% false positive rate to account for outdated records, unclear voter rolls or a dip in data quality needed to protect voter identities, Rocco said.

In this context, a false positive means that data between two sources has identified a noncitizen voter because of incomplete records between databases, not because they're actually a noncitizen.

More: Trump re-ups myth about Wisconsin voter numbers. Here are the facts

In this case, the Census Bureau said it used voter data from DataClear, a Virginia-based data collection firm, to help assemble the report.

By working with a third-party, the Census Bureau has to remove Social Security numbers, making cross-referencing with other data more difficult, according to Rocco. The bureau's report also doesn't say what voter rolls are being used, which means they could potentially be outdated.

The methodology is described in the brief: If a person appears in the voter database and does not have proof of citizenship, they're considered a noncitizen voter.

However, Rocco explained a potential problem using an example: You could have two people named John Smith living on Wisconsin Avenue with different birthdays. Without checking the data, there's no way to confirm whether those different birthdays mean there are actually two people or just a simple error.

Rocco said it's concerning that the Census report shows a roughly 0.02% noncitizen voter rate, or 24,000 out of 128 million voters examined, when the typical false positive rate is 1%-6%.

"This is an outlier in my experience," he said. "I have never seen a Census report that so clearly does not meet the standard of the bureau. The report is indistinguishable from having zero evidence."

Census report does not list authors

Rocco also pointed out the lack of authors listed on the report. The Census Bureau reliably lists authors on other publications, and even simple blog posts often have multiple credited authors, he said.

Without established authors, the question becomes whether Census staff or data were involved at all, Rocco said.

Barry Burden, director of UW-Madison's Elections Research Center, told the Associated Press that "the report is unsigned, is described merely as a 'beginning' analysis and relies on data from an unfamiliar private company."

"Necessary methodological details such as exactly how a ‘high-quality’ data match was defined are missing entirely," Burden said.
news.author: Journal Sentinel

news.title: Democrats don’t agree on how to talk about trans athletes. Just look at Ohio.
news.text:
This story on the debate over transgender athletes was originally reported by Amanda Becker of The 19th. Meet Amanda and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy.

It took mere minutes for the U.S. Supreme Court decision upholding state bans on trans athletes competing in women’s and girls’ sports to reverberate in Ohio’s competitive governor’s race — and the reactions from the Republican and Democratic nominees were all but indistinguishable.

“Ohio has barred men from competing with women in women’s sports and the Supreme Court now held that it’s constitutional,” Republican Vivek Ramaswamy told a Toledo newspaper.

Ramaswamy, a pharmaceutical entrepreneur, called the ruling “common sense” and pledged to enforce an Ohio law containing a ban on trans athletes in school-age sports. It was vetoed by the state’s current Republican Gov. Mike DeWine and opposed by every Democrat in the state legislature. 

Then, Democrat Dr. Amy Acton weighed in. 

“I do not support boys playing in girls sports. This is already settled law in Ohio, and as governor I will enforce and uphold the law,” the physician, who served as DeWine’s public health director, said in a statement to the same newspaper.

“As a doctor, public servant, and a mom, I will always stand up for fairness and protect kids’ health and safety,” she added.

Two candidates, from two different parties, taking the same public position, using the same language — wording favored by President Donald Trump’s MAGA movement that misgendered transgender athletes by referring to them as men instead of trans women. And in Acton’s case, language that misgendered trans children.

Related: Minnesota Republicans want trans girls out of girls sports, but complaints are hard to find

Democrats have been trying to figure out how to respond to Republicans’ anti-trans attacks since former Vice President Kamala Harris lost to Trump in the 2024 election. Republican campaigns and allied political groups spent more than $215 million that election cycle on ads targeting Democratic candidates’ past support for trans people and LGBTQ+ issues, according to data from AdImpact, which tracks political ad spending. In the final weeks of the campaign, tens of millions of dollars worth of these ads targeting Harris blanketed key suburbs in battleground states. They ended with the line: “Kamala is for they/them; President Trump is for you.” Harris never figured out how to respond. Internal research from the top super PAC supporting Harris showed that the “they/them” ads, on average, moved viewers 2.7 points in Trump’s favor. 

The conversation among Democrats about how the party’s candidates should — or should not — respond to anti-trans attacks has since taken up a lot of oxygen in Washington as party strategists debate the best course forward. 

Now, the conversation is consuming Democrats in Ohio. 

Acton’s initial statement on the day of the Supreme Court ruling landed like a lead balloon with the state’s LGBTQ+ groups and leaders, the vast majority of whom were enthusiastic about her candidacy and the potential to beat Ramaswamy, who said during a GOP presidential primary debate in late 2023 that being trans was a “mental health disorder.”

Several Ohio-based LGBTQ+ leaders told The 19th that they expected to hear more from the candidate herself. They hoped she might clean up the inarticulate language she used misgendering trans children, or offer additional reassurances to LGBTQ+ Ohioans that she would have their backs.

But no public or private reassurances came. 

Equality Ohio, one of the state’s largest groups working to protect the rights of LGBTQ+ people, updated Acton’s status on its 2026 Candidate Scorecard to “pending” from an “A” grade. 

Ramaswamy’s “F” rating has remained unchanged.

“This reflects our belief that accountability is still possible, and that the door remains open at this time. Should Dr. Acton choose to take meaningful steps forward, we will update the status accordingly,” the group said in a statement.

The ratings change was announced during what was initially branded as a “conversation” between Acton’s campaign, the state party and LGBTQ+ stakeholders that only further inflamed the situation. The meeting — and its fallout — was first reported by the Buckeye Flame, a Cleveland-based news site focused on Ohio’s LGBTQ+ community. 

The vice chair of the Ohio Democratic Party’s Pride Caucus, who is trans, was not admitted to the meeting and had to participate on speakerphone via the chair. It quickly became clear that it was less a conversation than a chance for participants to air concerns without any response from the campaign, attendees told The 19th. One described Acton’s campaign manager, Philip Stein, as “looking like someone who wanted to crawl under the table.”

Another participant said they went into the meeting thinking it could be a “teachable moment” that could repair relations between the campaign and Ohio’s LGBTQ+ community; they left feeling like the misgendering of trans children was intentional and a “cynical, consultant-driven play” to appeal to conservative voters.

“It felt like they were trying to throw trans people under the bus to provoke a backlash,” the person added. 

Related: Federal policy changes put gender-affirming care for youth at risk 

Meeting participants who spoke to The 19th all asked to not be identified because the campaign has told them that talking to the press precludes future conversations. 

Acton’s campaign wrote in an email to The 19th that she “will always stand up for Ohioans, including the LGBT community. As governor, she is committed to standing up to discrimination and ensuring all Ohioans receive equal protection under the law.”

More than 11 percent of Ohio’s adult population is LGBTQ+, according to an analysis released this month by the Human Rights Campaign, and research shows that queer people vote at higher rates than the overall adult public. While LGBTQ+ voters tend to favor Democrats, participants on the Zoom call told The 19th that the fallout would likely dampen queer voters’ willingness to support Acton by donating money, putting signs in their yards, going door-to-door in the final push or phonebanking.

Recent opinion polls show Acton and Ramaswamy nearly tied, trading single-digit leads well within polls’ margins of error. 

Governors are uniquely positioned to defend or reject anti-trans bills: Congress remains deadlocked on all but the most pressing, must-pass legislation; the U.S. Supreme Court decided that state-legislature passed bans on trans athletes in sports can stand. 

The law at issue in Ohio, H.B. 68, also prohibits minors from receiving gender-affirming care. DeWine vetoed it for that reason, but the GOP supermajority in the state legislature overrode his veto. The legality of the ban on gender-affirming care is a live question before the state Supreme Court. 

Acton, in an interview with The 19th following the U.S. Supreme Court ruling but before the campaign’s Zoom meeting with LGBTQ+ leaders, offered a more nuanced position on the law than she has shared publicly:

“This is a political battle,” Acton said, “and sadly, people are using people’s healthcare and personal decisions and choices as a way to pit us intentionally against one another, and it has been a successful tactic politically to scare people and frighten everyday Ohioans.”

“I’m also here to fight for our common humanity,” she continued. “The governor vetoed pretty draconian legislation, and the way he did that is he took advice from folks: I, amongst many people, gave advice. He listened to families. As governor, I will always research issues, listen to the absolute best experts in the field, as he did, talk to families and understand their personal decisions and what’s going on with their healthcare, with their physicians.”

She added that Democrats needed to break the GOP supermajority in the statehouse so gubernatorial vetoes could not be overridden. 

Related: Roller derby was already queer-friendly. Then it got more inclusive.

Acton’s campaign did not explain why she has not incorporated a more holistic approach to LGBTQ+ issues, like the one she described to The 19th, during campaign trail discussions. The campaign, as well as Acton herself, often point out that she is trying to become the first Democrat to lead Ohio in 15 years. A single Ohio Supreme Court justice is the only elected Democrat in statewide office; Ramaswamy is a billionaire self-funding his campaign with the backing of Peter Thiel, a tech billionaire and Trump ally. 

Still, Acton’s public statement on trans athletes puts her at the conservative end of an array of approaches being taken by Democrats on issues impacting trans people in the country’s five most competitive gubernatorial races. 

In Georgia, which has a ban on trans athletes competing in public school and college sports, Keisha Lance Bottoms is trying to flip the governor’s seat for Democrats in a race against Republican healthcare executive Rick Jackson. Shortly after the Supreme Court ruling, Bottoms’ campaign told a local news outlet that, as a mother, she “understands that there are important differences between male and female athletes in competitive sports. However, Keisha believes decisions about athletic participation should be made by appropriate athletic governing bodies — not by politicians.” Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, also told a local editorial board regarding gender-affirming care: “I do not believe the government should weigh in on medical decisions by Georgians and their physicians,” and that those decisions should not be “dictated by politicians looking to score political points.” Nearly every reliable poll has shown Bottoms ahead of Jackson since they won their respective primaries.

In Wisconsin, term-limited Democratic Gov. Tony Evers has repeatedly blocked bans related to trans athletes and gender-affirming care from taking effect. Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, the Democratic nominee for governor, has said that decisions regarding trans athletes should be left up to the state’s high school athletics association. He told HuffPost: “We don’t have to throw out our morals, our ethics … we don’t have to capitulate and get involved in these cultural wars Republicans try to throw out there because they don’t have anything to run on.” Polling conducted after the state’s August 12 primaries shows Crowley with a slight lead over his Republican opponent, U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, who is also a small business owner.

In Nevada, where sitting Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo tried but failed to get a “Protect Girls’ Sports” initiative onto 2026 ballots, Democratic Attorney General and gubernatorial candidate Aaron Ford has differentiated between his own beliefs and how he would govern. “I personally do not support trans athletes competing in sports opposite their gender assigned at birth,” Ford told a Nevada newspaper, using language preferred by LGBTQ+ rights groups. “But let’s be clear, Lombardo doesn’t care about this issue; he’s only using it as a political ploy to drum up support for his flailing reelection campaign.” Polls show Lombardo with a lead in the race. 

In Iowa, Democrat Rob Sand responded with a simple “no” when a conservative radio host asked him in May 2025 whether “biological males” should play women’s sports — another way to describe trans women that many in the LGBTQ+ community find offensive. But Sand, the state’s auditor, has also backed protections for trans people. He said at a town hall that it was “wrong” for Iowa Republicans to repeal state civil rights protections for trans people — Iowa was the first state in the country to do so. “You should not be fired from your job in the state of Iowa for being different. You should not be evicted from your apartment,” Sand said. Polls have for months shown Sand with a lead over Republican businessman Zach Lahn. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report last week moved the Iowa gubernatorial contest from the “toss up” category to “leans Democratic” in its competitiveness rankings.

John Neffinger, a Democratic strategist and past communications director for the Democratic National Committee, said Democrats should remember that, beyond sports, a majority of voters believe trans people should be protected from discrimination. Candidates shouldn’t be afraid to highlight their desire to support basic protections for LGBTQ+ people, he added. 

Polling consistently shows, for example, that more than half of voters prefer the Democratic Party’s approach to handling issues impacting trans people over solutions offered by the Republican Party. That includes polls conducted by Fox News. 

The political challenge for Democratic candidates is that nearly three-quarters of American adults say they are “uncomfortable” with trans athletes competing on sports teams that align with their gender identities, according to data from the nonpartisan Pew Research Center. Republicans have used Democrats’ past pro-LGBTQ+ stances to highlight this perceived vulnerability with voters in widespread attack ads. The dynamic has put many battleground Democratic candidates in between a voting populace not ready to largely embrace trans athletes in kids’ sports and many LGBTQ+ and progressive groups that want candidates to offer full-throated support for trans people as they face existential threats from the Trump administration.

In focus groups of a dozen or so undecided voters, Neffinger said, there might be one person who objects to LGBTQ+ protections on moral grounds, but the vast majority show a high level of empathy for the challenges trans people face in public life — especially trans children and their parents. 

“When you talk about sports, what you get from people is, ‘Now, that’s not right,’” Neffinger said. “But even then, they don’t want politicians picking on kids, they get that that’s not cool.”

For several years now, Neffinger has been in a cohort of Democratic strategists trying to help and encourage the party’s candidates and lawmakers to figure out how to meet Republicans’ anti-trans attacks head on. There are ways for candidates to walk the line between where the average voter is and where LGBTQ+ and other progressive advocacy groups want them to be, he said. They just have to be willing to do it.

Neffinger pointed to a 2025 statement from Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto shortly after the Nevada Democrat voted against the Republican-offered Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act as an effective example of messaging that resonates with middle-of-the-road voters. 

Cortez Masto’s statement read: “I support fair play and safety and do not support transgender athletes competing in girls’ and women’s sports when it compromises those principles. I believe local schools, student athletes, coaches, and parents are much better equipped to implement fair, strong policies on this issue than politicians in Congress.”

Staking out a fairness-based position — for everyone — paves the way for politicians to offer different policy solutions as circumstances demand, Neffinger said. That could mean allowing prepubescent athletes to compete on teams that match their gender identities, or on a case-by-case basis permitting trans athletes who received gender-affirming care before going through puberty, he added. 

“Saying ‘no boys in girls sports’ feels like the latest way to dodge — ‘don’t make me talk about this.’ It doesn’t look like leadership, it looks like a cop-out, and it actually feels like you’re picking on trans kids,” he added. 

Democrats of all stripes — centrists, progressives and LGBTQ+ advocates — also point to the 2025 governor’s race in Virginia, when Democratic former Rep. Abigail Spanberger beat Republican Winsome Earle-Sears, the state’s former lieutenant governor who spent as much as $9 million attacking Spanberger’s support for trans rights. Spanberger beat Earle-Sears by more than 15 points, and by nearly 30 points in Loudoun County, an exurban area near Washington, D.C., where anti-trans ads were believed to have hurt Harris the year before. Harris won Virginia, but only by about 5 points. 

The various Democratic factions agree that what made Spanberger’s approach successful was that she introduced voters to her values early on, then took on anti-trans attacks as a matter of discrimination. Spanberger also emphasized that parents and doctors should make decisions for children, and she took voters’ concerns about fairness in sports seriously.

“Leaders must take a joint approach: fiercely defending LGBTQI+ people from discrimination and advocating for policies that will lift up families across the country,” the Center for American Progress, a Democratic policy organization, concluded in a recent analysis that caused ripples in Washington by recommending the party’s base accept some restrictions on trans athletes in youth sports. 

Nan Whaley, the former Democratic mayor of Dayton, Ohio, and the party’s gubernatorial nominee in 2022, acknowledged that the political landscape related to LGBTQ+ issues has shifted to the right since her unsuccessful bid. She is an enthusiastic supporter of Acton and believes that, despite the falling out between her campaign and LGBTQ+ groups, voters should trust her. Whaley said that trans Ohioans have shared fears with her about their safety; some have asked whether she thinks they should leave the state, given its politics. 

“If Vivek Ramaswamy wins, I don’t know what I can say to them, but I know what I can say if Amy Acton is governor,” Whaley said. “That’s what’s at stake.”
news.summary:
Dr. Amy Acton's Trump-like statement in the governor’s race raises questions about how far candidates in battleground states can go before jeopardizing LGBTQ+ support.

news.title: Jelly Roll Says Trump Jokes Are Your Fault: 'You Should've Voted For' Harris
news.text:
On Monday, Jimmy Kimmel Live! guest host Jelly Roll called President Trump a racist and told several fat jokes, which naturally led to him being criticized on the internet. On Tuesday, he returned to the ABC show to attack those critics and say if you wanted “jokes about Kamala Harris, you should've voted for her.”

My ‘ball room’ is an absolute disaster. Thank you, Cletones. You know what? I did a couple jokes like that last night, because I'm hosting a damn late night show. That's where you talk about the news and you make jokes, but, I guess, apparently because I did it, it really messed with people's heads. Some folks online were upset that I didn't treat the president with reverence and dignity. But I want to remind you, I go by the name Jelly Roll. I don't even treat myself with reverence and dignity. One day I looked in the mirror and said, ‘You, my friend, are a pastry.’”
