news.title: This Mississauga artist creates provocative images based on the U.S. flag: 'We’re so numb to the idiocy'
news.text:
“There are so many things I love that are American,” Gary Taxali told the Star from his Mississauga home studio. “I love jazz and Frank Lloyd Wright, and Andy Warhol is my favourite artist.”

But when it comes to flag design, Taxali — one of Canada’s most celebrated illustrators, who leveraged his background in advertising into international gallery shows and fingerprints on virtually every corner of pop culture — is an avowed homer.

“I think that the Canadian flag is superior as a piece of graphic design to the U.S.,” Taxali said. “That’s my honest opinion.”

The visual contrast between the Maple Leaf and the Stars and Stripes — and the way that esthetic tension ties to contemporary political and ideological frictions — has inflected several of Taxali’s recent commissions; such broad iconography suits his slyly modernist style.

One cartoon for the American political magazine The Nation depicts the True North Strong and Free as a pair of legs kicking a Trumpian silhouette up and out of frame; it’s called “Message from Canada.” Another image posted to Instagram features a shoe branded with l’Unifolié stepping on and shattering Old Glory; it’s captioned “We Will Never Be Your 51st State.”

“A couple of years ago, if you’d said that an American president was going to make Canada a target, people would have asked you, ‘What Terry Gilliam movie did you just watch?’ Like, that would have been too absurd,” the artist said. “Now it’s just normal. We’re watching it in real time. How did this happen in our lifetimes?

“We’re so numb to the idiocy of what we’re watching on a daily basis.”

This fall, Taxali is releasing a collection of his flag-based artworks, dubbed succinctly, and suggestively, “Flagged,” a title that hints simultaneously at keeping tabs on a deteriorating situation and experiencing fatigue with the whole thing — an uncomfortable numbness requiring the prodding of an artist’s pen.

The timing is apt considering the upcoming U.S. midterm elections; like any good satirist, Taxali is trying to seize and influence his moment. But there are entries in “Flagged” that can’t help but feel dated despite their righteous intentions, like the Pop Art posters Taxali created in support of Kamala Harris — hypothetically triumphal emblems for a campaign that came up short.

“I can take anybody on and make it work,” said Taxali, who rejects the idea that the 2024 Democratic presidential candidate was a tough sell in terms of imagery. “I did one where I had the flag in a vertical format. There are seven stars and stripes and (Kamala) has seven letters. I used that and people went nuts. Lots of Americans were waving my Kamala flag.”

He does acknowledge, though, that Trump’s visuals have become so iconic that they’re difficult to dislodge. “It’s hard to compete with ‘Make America Great Again,’” he said. “I mean, in terms of that iconography — the red hat, the white letters. It’s some pretty kick-ass branding.”

He had a cap he was selling in both red and blue with the image of Harris stepping on the red hat. “And I had Americans messaging me to say that they were afraid to buy the red one because they were worried about being perceived as MAGA from a distance,” he said.

‘It’s a form of protection’

In 2025, Greenpeace commissioned Taxali to create an artwork in solidarity with the “Elbows Up” movement, which he still thinks in retrospect was a clever and expressive bit of political rhetoric. “Elbows Up is great,” he said. “Anything that was an antidote to what they were hurling at us, I thought was good. It’s a form of protection … it’s not like you’re going to whack somebody with your stick. You’re just trying to keep your opponent off of you so you can score a goal.”

For all his interest in estheticizing Canadian strength, however, Taxali isn’t simply or strictly patriotic. Like any good satirist, he’s sensitive to complexity even if his fans sometimes are not.

“In July, I did an image where I had the Canadian flag and the top of it was pointier than normal, and I added two dots for eyes, and people lost their s—t,” said Taxali. “They said, ‘Wait a second, we’re not the racist country full of white supremacists.’ I thought, ‘Talk to a brown or black or Indigenous person and they might tell you otherwise.’ People who’d followed me for a long time didn’t want to go there.

“It’s not like America has a monopoly on racism.”

Seeing things through his eyes

It’s a fine line between images that prompt reflection and ones that tell viewers how to think, and Taxali, who’s also an instructor at OCAD University, said he’s preoccupied by questions of artistic legibility as well as media literacy.

“I teach illustration,” he said, “And I tell my students that the pictures they make are nothing without the text, and the meaning and the message. They’re intrinsically connected because they’re communicating an idea.” The more nuanced and layered the idea, he added, the more sophisticated the image will be.

“I also tell my students that we’re not just drawing pictures; we need a frame of reference. Which means they need to read more. Read more articles. And read things you disagree with, so that you can disagree with them.”

Taxali’s consistency and productivity across a variety of media and platforms is impressive. He’s driven by a desire to invite others to see things through his eyes. “When I was a little kid, the local community centre had an art contest to promote their swimming pool,” he recalled.

“They were looking for a poster, and I thought I could do something with people and fish, all of these funny things. I came in third place, I think, but I was so proud of the fact that somebody actually looked at what I did and thought it was worth putting on a wall. It made me feel pretty good.”
news.author: Adam Nayman

news.title: Why Gush Over Abdul el-Sayed Taking on 'Fox's Outrage Machine'?
news.text:
On August 24, controversial Democrat Senate candidate Abdul el-Sayed boldly accepted an invitation to the Fox News show Jesse Watters Primetime. It oozed confidence, but whether it was smart or strategic to play the Artful Dodger is a very different question.

In his newsletter, CNN media analyst Brian Stelter gushed over el-Sayed generating “lots of buzz and clippable content” and how he “showed a keen understanding of Fox’s outrage machine.” This is always amusing, as if Stelter doesn’t think CNN can be characterized as operating an “outrage machine” against Trump.

Then Stelter mischaracterized the central mishap of the interview. El-Sayed was credited for “refusing to take the bait when Watters asked whether it’s okay ‘for a parent to slash his kid’s ding-a-ling off’ or whether trans athletes should compete in women’s sports. Each time, he redirected toward gas and grocery prices, the war in Iran, and health care.”

That’s not what happened. When Watters pressed him on genital amputations for children, he insisted this decision is between a doctor and a patient, and the government should not get involved – which is a bizarre position when you’re pushing for a “Medicare for All” scheme where the government controls the health care system.

When Watters kept pressing, el-Sayed asked the host “Do you really wanna have this conversation? Are you circumcised?” What kind of oafish inquiry is that? Then he pressed: “So you should want to move on.” That’s not answering the question. It’s an attempt to shut down the line of inquiry by getting personal.

Watters felt compelled to point out to the guy who went to an Ivy League medical school that “circumcision is different than castration.” El-Sayed just repeated “It's a problem that you think that you get to decide what happens between a parent, a doctor, and a patient.” That’s a questionable position, since El-Sayed fervently supported Covid lockdowns and vaccine mandates five years ago.

The host shifted into the scandal of boys playing in girls’ sports, and that’s when the Democrat started leaning into the high prices and the war, “the issues people actually care about in Michigan.” Watters pointed out that the interview started with gas prices and the so-called “Green New Deal.”

Stelter touted similar analysis from a fellow liberal at The New York Times. Bayliss Wagner wrote El-Sayed’s strategy was “to cast ‘culture-war’ issues as a distraction from the everyday problems Americans face, like rising costs and worries about health care.”

The Left loves to play this dishonest game: “Culture wars” only start when conservatives resist the leftist crusade, and it’s only a “distraction” when the Left doesn’t win without a fight. They know the transgender issue was a reason Kamala Harris lost, so they want to dodge the issue.

Stelter concluded by telling readers to “beware the algorithmic distortion,” with conservatives “celebrating Watters for dunking on El-Sayed and exposing Democratic ‘extremism.’” They always pretend no Democrat position is extreme. Stelter added his CNN colleague Andrew Kirell “saw post after post from liberals applauding El-Sayed for showing how to handle Fox — by engaging and knowing all their tricks.”

Stelter and his media colleagues are only grading el-Sayed on his tactical dodging skills around Fox “tricks.” They’re not examining how voters may want to know where the Democrat stands on amputations for kids, or boys in girls’ sports. Candidates for office should have identifiable positions, not just dismiss “distractions.”

This is the same Stelter who hailed Sen. Jon Ossoff’s “art of the viral clip” for recklessly smearing White House aide Natalie Harp as Trump’s new girlfriend. Why must they only judge tactics and not judge on the facts?

news.title: The second Dan Sullivan makes the general election in Alaska’s Senate race
news.text: Former teacher Dan J. Sullivan will join Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic challenger Mary Peltola on the general election ballot in Alaska’s Senate race, NBC News projects. Republicans have criticized the other Sullivan’s candidacy as a potential ploy to confuse voters in a key battleground race, which he has denied. Alaska’s election system might also blunt the impact of any confusion. The top four candidates, regardless of party, advance from Alaska’s all-party primary to a ranked-choice general election, meaning voters could rank both Sullivans. But some voters end up ranking only one candidate, which could matter in a close race — and Alaska’s Senate race could be one of the closest in the country this year. Democrats have targeted Alaska as an opportunity to flip a seat since well before the same-name saga consumed the race, even though President Donald Trump carried the state by double digits in each of the last three presidential elections. Peltola, a former state legislator and city council member, became the first Alaska Native to represent the state in Congress when she won a statewide special election in 2022 and then a full term months later. Peltola lost her seat after one term by 3 percentage points, running well ahead of Vice President Kamala Harris at the top of the Democratic ticket in 2024. Sullivan was first elected to the Senate in 2014, defeating a Democratic incumbent, and re-elected in 2020. A former Marine, he has touted his work for veterans and the state’s fishing industry. His campaign and Republican allies have criticized the other Sullivan as a potential Democratic plant, noting that he only recently registered as a Republican and got help with his campaign launch from a Democratic consultant. State and federal prosecutors are investigating whether his candidacy is part of a conspiracy to confuse voters. The federal investigation is moving forward, with a law enforcement official telling NBC News that a grand jury issued subpoenas last week to compel information from witnesses related to the Dan J. Sullivan campaign. The candidate told The New York Times that he registered as a Republican because his previous political party, the Alaska Independence Party, no longer exists. He declined to detail his involvement with the Democratic consultant because of the ongoing investigation.
news.summary: NBC News projects that GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan and Republican Dan J. Sullivan will face off in the general election alongside former Rep. Mary Peltola, a Democrat.

news.title: Trump wins again. Takeaways from Darline Graham's SC primary victory
news.text:
President Donald Trump's endorsement proved essential for South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham's South Carolina special runoff Senate primary win, which was very much in doubt before the Aug. 25 primary.

After Trump recruited Graham to serve out the remainder of her late brother Lindsey Graham's term, Trump pleaded in person with Republican voters in the Palmetto State to send Graham to the November general election at an Aug. 21 campaign rally in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina. And they followed his command.

"The thing that hammered it home was his visit and telling the MAGA crowd that his endorsement was unequivocal," Scott Huffmon, a political science professor at Winthrop University, told USA TODAY. "Trump left no doubt who he was behind, and they voted the way he told them to, period." That led the Trump-endorsed incumbent and political neophyte to beat hardline conservative Rep. Ralph Norman in the heavily Republican state, 52% to 48%, the Associated Press and NBC News projected.

Experts had labeled the race a toss-up and an Aug. 24 poll showed the two contenders tied at 48% each.

"We did it!" Graham told supporters during her victory speech. "I have mixed emotions right now. I'm still feeling grief, heartache, and immense gratitude. Thank you all again."

The gratitude also included thanking Trump for making it happen, with Graham adding that South Carolina "is truly Trump Country."

Whether Graham is prepared or not for the job will be the next test in the deeply red state, Danielle Vinson, a politics and international affairs professor at Furman University, told USA TODAY. "Her entire campaign is 'I will follow Donald Trump’s agenda,' Vinson said about Graham. "That’s been her message. Why should she stop now?"

Here are the key takeaways from Tuesday's pivotal primary.

Trump's endorsement gave Graham 'a pretty solid win'

Trump stressed the importance of Graham winning at the Aug. 21 campaign rally. He urged supporters to vote for Graham and wanted them to "pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot. Just come and vote. It’s so important."

"The MAGA support came out in full force," Huffmon said, especially in Horry County, where Trump visited in Myrtle Beach.

"As the votes were coming in, it became obvious she was going to win," Huffmon said. "It wasn’t microscopic; it wasn't overwhelming, but it’s a pretty solid win over a proven candidate."

Darline Graham in focus: What to know about the South Carolina GOP Senate candidate

Although Norman won the populous Greenville County, he really couldn’t expand his support base beyond his own congressional district in upstate South Carolina, Vinson said. "Norman couldn’t make inroads further south and east of the state," Vinson said. "He simply couldn't appeal to them."

Huffmon said Graham's name recognition helped, "but clearly, and I can't say it enough, the full-throated, unequivocal Trump endorsement and visit gave her a clear victory." 

Graham's win only adds to Trump's near-perfect primary success rate for his endorsed Republican candidates, including Georgia Senate nominee Mike Collins, Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton and New York congressional nominee Anthony Constantino, according to Ballotpedia, an online elections website.

Trump got more endorsement magic on Aug. 25 as his pick for Oklahoma governor, former state Sen. Mike Mazzei, defeated state Attorney General Gentner Drummond in a Republican primary runoff.

Did the 'I'm not a polished politician' gaffe hurt Graham?

Based on her runoff win, voters may not mind Graham's lack of political experience, even after Graham was asked during a debate whether Taiwan and the South China Sea are important national security interests for the United States. 

"I’m not that informed on national security, so — but I do support the military," Graham said. "I'm not a polished politician up here. National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise, but I do support the military."

The misstep didn't matter, this time, and probably won't going forward, Vinson, the Furman University professor, said.

"We don’t seem to care," Vinson said. "But Trump isn’t polished, either, and he’s won three times in this state. I guess we have some South Carolina voters who prefer unpolished nonpoliticians." 

Still, Graham has to become more adept, Huffmon, the Winthrop University professor said, although she will be the favorite against Democratic nominee and political novice Annie Andrews, who has been campaigning for more than a year in the heavily Republican state.

"Mistakes will happen, but she really has to try really hard not to make gaffes in her debates anymore," Huffmon said.

What lies ahead for Graham

During her victory speech, Graham couldn't wait to take shots at Andrews, calling her opponent "the most radical liberal ever nominated for a statewide office" by the South Carolina Democratic Party, comparing her views to those of Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vermont, and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D- New York.

"If you like Kamala Harris for President, then you're going to love Dr. Annie Andrews," Graham said, saying conservative South Carolina cannot allow "Democratic socialists to take a foothold" in their state.

Andrews is running on a platform of improving healthcare access, including expanding the Affordable Care Act (ACA) health insurance (also known as Obamacare) coverage for more South Carolinians and bolstering public health agencies.

"I am not a socialist. I find it really entertaining that they have nothing to attack me on and are resorting to the same old Republican Party talking points," Andrews said on MS NOW after hearing Graham's comments. "I don't know what's so radical about thinking everyone in this state has access to affordable health care, to be able to see a doctor when they need one? I don't see what's so radical about thinking that every county in South Carolina should have an OBGYN? I don't know what's so radical about families who are working hard to be able to put food on the table and also keep their lights on at the end of the month?

"If that's the best Darline has, I think it's going to be a fun and exciting 70 days ahead as we continue to work to build a coalition to flip South Carolina blue in November," Andrews added.

Vinson believes Democrats have put up the right challenger in Andrews, as she's seeking to capture young voters, first-timers, moderates, independents, and those who believe their cost of living has become unbearable.

"Regardless of her chances of winning, she’s generating some enthusiasm," Vinson said. "She also will have to win some Republican voters to stand a chance. That's a tall order."

But that could make the Senate race more intriguing, especially against another political novice such as Graham, Vinson said. Andrews has prior campaign experience. In 2022, she ran against Rep. Nancy Mace in South Carolina's 1st Congressional District and lost by 14 percentage points.

That could come in handy for Andrews, compared to Graham, who has been mostly guarded throughout the Republican primary races.

"She cannot hide behind that lack of experience," Vinson said about Graham. "She can’t insulate herself in the general election campaign; it will be really evident against someone like Annie Andrews."

Huffmon thinks Graham has to force Andrews to scrape votes away from her.

"She needs to stick to her talking points, the Republican talking points; She’s pretty safe," Huffmon said. "At this point in South Carolina's history, nuance isn’t as important as it is in purple states."

Graham has to be more prepared, and maybe even show a bit more of her personality beyond her Trump talking points, even if she's the favorite to win, Vinson concluded.

"The sentimentality may only go so far," Vinson said.

news.title: Taylor Swift, Beyonce and other celebrities react to death of Dolly Parton
news.text:
Celebrities and politicians are offering their condolences following the death of country music superstar Dolly Parton, who died Tuesday at the age of 80.

President Donald Trump wrote on social media that he would be lowering the American flag for one week in honor of Parton, calling her death "a true loss for millions of people."

"There has never been anyone like her, and never will," Trump wrote.

"Dolly Parton: An American Original - A Special Edition of 20/20" airs Tuesday, Aug. 25, at 10 p.m. ET on ABC and streams the next day on Disney+ and Hulu.

"A world without Dolly doesn’t feel possible, real, or right. But because of the eternally generous way she spent her time on this earth and the countless lives she changed for the better, her legacy will be an everlasting one," Taylor Swift said in a lengthy statement.

"She was truly the gift that kept on giving. Dolly gave us someone to look up to while encouraging us to be who we are as individuals," the statement continued. "Somehow she was able to give us her lessons about the world gently and honestly, simultaneously, and oftentimes hilariously. She managed to give the world the ultimate mystery and fantasy in some corners of her life, but to give full transparency in the ways that counted. Somehow she was true grace and true grit, all in one dazzling person. She possessed the softest heart when it came to the struggles of others, and a backbone of steel to defend her own self worth as an artist."

Swift said she was grateful for Parton's music and philanthropy and saluted the music legend "For the tightropes she walked so that young girls like me could grow up dreaming of joining the circus too."

Beyoncé honored the "Queen of Country" in a heartfelt message shared on her official website.

"You were the barometer. The North Star. Bold and brilliant. Talented and tenacious. You taught so many lessons on how to be uniquely oneself," Beyoncé wrote. "I am grateful for your art, your heart, your generosity, your humor, your entrepreneurship. I'm honored that I had the privilege to work with you."

"You are truly one of one. Rest peacefully," she added.

Sabrina Carpenter, who collaborated with Parton on a version of "Please Please Please" from Carpenter's "Short n' Sweet" deluxe album, remembered Parton as "an angel walking the earth."

"I will cherish our laughter and conversations and i will keep your wisdom, your playful outlook on life, and perfect sense of humor in my pocket for the rainy days," Carpenter wrote on Instagram. "there will never be another you and how lucky are we all to have experienced your singular magic as well as your once in a lifetime voice, songs, and heart."

"your light will be something the world will search forever to find again 🦋🦋🦋 i will always love you," she added.

Jane Fonda, Parton's friend and co-star in the 1980 hit comedy "9 to 5," wrote on Instagram, "I am devastated."

"Dolly will always be with us because she was so present, so powerful, so generous and playful that she is woven into all our lives and hearts forever," Fonda wrote. "We have our memories of her, her songs, Dollywood, '9to5,' the millions of books she got into the hands of children, all the iconic images that bring her to us. And they are all blessings. Let's be grateful for all that she has left us to ease our sadness now."

"... To her gay and trans fans, I want you to know that she loved you," Fonda added. " ... And you know she doesn't want y'all to mourn now. Dress up and celebrate her spirit."

Lily Tomlin, Parton's longtime friend and her other "9 to 5" co-star, wrote on Instagram, "No words ... 💔."

The movie was Parton's big-screen debut, and she wrote and performed the film's chart-topping, Grammy-winning theme song.

Tomlin said at the 16th Annual Governors Awards in 2025 that the song "9 to 5" was "so much bigger than any singular theme song on a movie soundtrack," saying it "became an anthem for our culture of the time."

She added at the time that Parton's "humanitarian achievements are as staggering as her formidable singing career" and called her "one of the few people who remains in this world that everyone loves and respects."

Country singer Kacey Musgraves wrote on social media on Tuesday, "This really really hurts."

"The world feels a lot less sparkly all of a sudden," Musgraves said, adding, "So glad she's with her Carl Dean."

Dean, who was Parton's husband of nearly 60 years, died last year at the age of 82.

Parton's fellow country singer and actress Reba McEntire wrote on Instagram, "Dolly, thank you for all the wonderful things you did for us here on earth. Your love, your music and you gave so much with your huge huge heart."

"There will never ever be another you. We will remember and cherish every memory and every note you ever played and sang," she continued. "... I'll never forget the first time I met you and I'll never forget our last conversation. I hold it with love in my heart."

Former President Barack Obama reflected on Parton's life and wide-ranging impact in a statement on X.

"It's hard to imagine many people having a bigger impact than Dolly Parton," Obama wrote. "Born in a one-room cabin, she earned 11 Grammys and an Emmy, built a business empire, helped millions of kids learn to read, and — as if that wasn't enough — helped accelerate the research that led to the Moderna COVID vaccine. What a life."

"Michelle and I are thinking of Dolly's family and her many, many fans," he added.

Former President George W. Bush also remembered Parton as both an entertainer and philanthropist.

"Laura and I, along with thousands of her fans, mourn the passing of Dolly Parton. We loved her music and her style. She was a great entertainer and even greater person," Bush said in a statement shared by the George W. Bush Presidential Center on X.

"We respected her work to promote literacy, advance health, and strengthen communities. Dolly was a talented and hardworking American who will be missed," he added.

Former President Bill Clinton described Parton as "a great songwriter and performer who told the stories of everyday Americans with honesty, humility, and heart."

"She rose high from her East Tennessee roots and never forgot where she came from. And she always believed in giving back, especially in her efforts to promote literacy," he wrote in a statement. "Hillary and I were big fans and first saw her in 1974, and will always be grateful for the music and the memories. Our thoughts and prayers are with her family, her legion of fans, and everyone who loved her."

Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton added, "Dolly Parton did all the good she could, for all the people she could, for as long as ever she could. From her legendary songwriting to the Imagination Library -- which sent 1 million books a month to children across the country -- she was the best of America. Dolly, we'll miss your great heart."

The Jacksons called Parton a "true trailblazer" in a statement on Instagram.

"Through her extraordinary talent, kindness and generosity, she opened doors and inspired generations around the world. We share this special memory from 1977, when we had the honor of meeting Dolly in England on the same day we also met Queen Elizabeth II," the Jacksons wrote alongside a carousel of images. "Thank you, Dolly, for the music, the joy and the light you shared with us all."

"Our prayers are with Dolly's family, friends and everyone whose life she touched. ... Your beautiful spirit and remarkable legacy will live on forever," the Jacksons said.

Comedian and actress Carol Burnett took to social media to reflect on one of her "favorite memories," taping the "Dolly & Carol in Nashville" special in Parton's home state of Tennessee.

"We shot the week of Thanksgiving and Dolly made individual turkey dinners for every one of us, that she cooked herself," Burnett said.

"That's who she was," she said, adding, "I'm so sad right now." 

Former Vice President Kamala Harris called Parton a "true American icon" in a statement Tuesday.

"Her career accolades included 11 Grammy awards, an Emmy, an honorary Oscar, and -- my favorite -- more than 300 million books sent to millions of children around the world through her Imagination Library," Harris wrote. "All at once she was kind, modest, and funny. With her music, her philanthropy, and her style, Dolly was one of one."

"Doug and I send our prayers to her family, friends, and all those who have been touched by her magic," she said. "We will always love you, Dolly."

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee said Parton was "one of a kind, who loved people, her work, her family, and her Lord."

"Tennessee has forever been changed -- enhanced -- by her, and will never be quite the same without Dolly," the governor said on social media.

Reese Witherspoon wrote on social media, "When I was playing June Carter Cash in 'Walk the Line,' [Parton] took me to dinner and told me stories of how June Carter charmed everyone in country music. Dolly gave me the courage to put my whole spirit into that performance and made me see how lucky I was to be a storyteller."

Witherspoon said throughout her career, Parton sent her "notes of encouragement and support, telling me to be the light in people's lives and listen to my angels."

"Dolly, I miss you already. Your talent, your wisdom and your beautiful spirit lit up our lives," the actress said.

Khloe Kardashian, a Parton superfan, wrote in an Instagram story post, "Some people are so extraordinary, their existence feels almost impossible. Dolly was one of those people."

"A once-in-a-lifetime soul. A woman whose light, heart, talent and humanity changed this world forever," Kardashian wrote. "To have admired her was a gift. To have met her, spent time in her presence, and somehow been lucky enough that Dolly Parton knew my name... I will never have words big enough for what that means to me."

"What an astronomical human being. What a legacy. What a loss," she added. "There will never be another Dolly."

Singer Kelly Clarkson also honored the legendary singer, writing on social media that Parton "had a way of making everyone feel special, and seen, and welcomed, and as if you were old friends."

"I will miss her heart and her voice as I am sure millions will," Clarkson said. "What an incredible gift and talent she was and still is with an amazing catalogue of art she has left behind for all of us."

Jack White of The White Stripes, who covered Parton's hit song "Jolene" in 2000, posted a photo of Parton on Instagram with the caption, "Instant Sainthood."

Actress and singer Kristin Chenoweth wrote on Instagram that she was "heartbroken," calling Parton her "ultimate inspiration."

"I met Dolly on several occasions and she always made me feel like one of her own. She even agreed to sing with me on one of my records," Chenoweth said. "... The world has lost one of the best but I know we will never forget her because she is impossible to forget. I love you Dolly and I will ALWAYS love you."

The Muppets also honored the iconic performer, saying in a statement on Facebook, "There will never be another quite like Dolly Parton. She was the ultimate singer, songwriter, actress, performer, and philanthropist. She filled the world with light and we are so grateful for every second we got to spend with her onstage and off."

Actress Octavia Spencer called Parton "a gift to the world," writing on social media, [Y]our voice, your philanthropic heart, and warmth made us ... feel seen and that the world was a pretty decent place."

Actor Colman Domingo wrote on social media, "Dolly taught us that you can be anything and do anything and to do it with kindness. What a light. We are all grateful that we lived in a time of Dolly Parton. We will always love her."
news.summary: Celebrities and politicians are offering their condolences following the death of country music superstar Dolly Parton.
news.author: Emily Shapiro

news.title: Daughter of late House Dem loses runoff bid to finish father's term
news.text: Marcye Scott, the daughter of late Rep. David Scott, D-Ga., fell short Tuesday in her bid to succeed her father in Congress for the final few months of his term, despite leading the first-round of voting last month. Former teacher and Gwinnett County school board chairman Everton Blair defeated Scott in the special election runoff for the remainder of David Scott's term in Georgia’s heavily Democratic 13th Congressional District, which covers parts of metro Atlanta. Blair will hold the seat only through early January, when the winner of November’s regularly scheduled general election takes office. Blair also ran in the primary to compete for a full-term, but lost to Democratic Georgia state representative Jasmine Clark in the primary earlier this year. Clark will battle Republican Jonathan Chavez in November for the seat, the official term for which will start in January 2027. AFTER LINDSEY GRAHAM'S DEATH, SISTER JOINS LONG LIST OF RELATIVES WHO REPLACED LATE FAMILY MEMBERS IN CONGRESS David Scott represented the district for more than two decades before dying April 22 at age 80. At the time of his death, he was seeking a 13th term and facing a competitive Democratic primary challenge from Clark and others. In 2024, he carried the district with roughly 72% of the vote, while then-Vice President Kamala Harris won about 71% there in the presidential race, compared with roughly 28% for President Donald Trump. UNEARTHED INTERVIEW EXPOSES DEM SENATOR'S PAST SUPPORT FOR REPARATIONS: 'THERE IS A DEBT UNPAID' Marcye Scott entered Tuesday’s runoff after leading the July 28 special election with roughly 46% of the vote, compared with about 38% for Blair, but fell short of the majority required to win outright, leading to the runoff against Blair. Blair's victory would restore voting representation to Georgia’s heavily Democratic 13th District and add another Democratic vote to the narrowly divided House for the final months of the 119th Congress. Georgia’s 13th District has been without voting representation since David Scott’s death, although his former congressional offices have remained open under the supervision of the House clerk to provide constituent services, according to the Office of the Clerk of the U.S. House of Representatives. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP According to his campaign's website, Blair earned graduate degrees from Stanford and Harvard, previously worked with the Obama administration’s White House Initiative on Educational Excellence and, in 2018, was the first Black and youngest-ever member elected to his county's school board.
news.summary: Marcye Scott fell short against former Gwinnett County school board chairman Everton Blair in her bid to finish the final months of her late father’s House term after leading the first round of voting.
news.author: Alec Schemmel

news.title: Everton Blair wins special election for late Rep. David Scott's seat
news.text: Residents of Georgia's 13th Congressional District selected Everton Blair to serve the remainder of Rep. David Scott's term after the longtime lawmaker's death in April, according to a projection from The Associated Press. Blair defeated Scott's daughter, Marcye Scott, in Tuesday's special election. Blair, the former chair of the Gwinnett County School Board, had finished second to Scott out of the five candidates during the July 28 nonpartisan special election. Both had then advanced to Tuesday's runoff. With his victory, Blair will only serve out the remaining few months of David Scott's final term, set to end in January, because he placed third in the May 19 Democratic primary for the full two-year term. In November, voters will decide whether Democratic state Rep. Jasmine Clark or Republican Jonathan Chavez will serve the full term beginning in January. The 13th District has typically been extremely favorable for Democratic candidates. Scott won his 2024 re-election bid with about 72% of the vote, and then-Vice President Kamala Harris received about 71% of the vote in the district.There are 70 days until the 2026 midterm elections.
news.summary: Everton Blair Jr. will serve out the remaining few months of the late Rep. David Scott's final term, the Associated Press projects.
news.author: Dan Raby
